household_task_division.observation: Grandmothers keep the fire and the smallest children while the strong go out, and each season has its own hands for its own work.

seasonal_work_round.observation: Planting, felling and building each get their own season, so no household is asked to do all three at once.

midday_heat_rest.observation: In the hot months work stops while the sun stands highest and starts again in the long shade of afternoon.

children_light_tasks.observation: Children too small for the hoe run the plots with clappers to scare the birds, and glean what the reapers missed.

herding_rotas.observation: Households take turns walking the common flock, so one boy watches forty animals instead of every family watching its own few.

work_party_feasts.observation: A family brews and cooks, the neighbours come to raise the roof, and everyone eats and drinks when it is done.
work_party_feasts.social_consequence: Jobs no household could finish alone are done in a day, and the feast that repays them binds neighbours in debt and pride.

festival_rest_days.observation: On the days of the great festivals no one is sent to the fields; tools are hung up and the whole village rests together.

part_time_specialists.observation: The potter's family still farms, but in the slack months its kiln burns for the whole village and is paid in grain.
part_time_specialists.social_consequence: Some households become known for pots or blades and trade that skill for food; the first differences of craft appear.

slack_season_building.observation: Walls go up after the harvest is in, when hands are idle and the ground is dry enough to dig.

household_craft_learning.observation: A girl sits at her mother's loom and a boy at his father's knapping stone until the motions are their own.

hauling_chants.observation: A caller sings the line and the whole team heaves on the answer, so the load moves at once and no one pulls alone.

great_work_parties.observation: Hundreds come from many villages to drag a great stone or throw up a dyke, fed for the season by the ones who called them.
great_work_parties.social_consequence: Whole districts can now raise a monument or a flood bank together, and whoever can call them out gains a new kind of standing.

full_time_specialists.observation: Smiths and potters who no longer farm draw their bread from the common store and give their whole year to the craft.
full_time_specialists.social_consequence: Specialists who never work the fields live off the shared store; the store and its keepers become the center of the town.

load_tallies.observation: The overseer cuts a notch for every basket carried up the bank, and at dusk the stick shows who worked and how much.

shrine_work_obligations.observation: Each household owes the shrine so many days of digging, building or reaping, and the priests keep count of who has given them.
shrine_work_obligations.social_consequence: The shrine's store is filled by owed days rather than gifts; the first labor obligation brings the first resentment of it.

fixed_worker_rations.observation: Every worker on the great estate is given the same measure of barley each day, in good years and in bad.
fixed_worker_rations.social_consequence: Workers are fed a fixed measure whatever the harvest, and those who hand out the grain decide who works.

craft_quarters.observation: Potters settle by potters and smiths by smiths, sharing clay pits, fuel yards and the secrets of the trade.

apprentice_for_keep.observation: A boy lives in the smith's house and works his bellows for bread and a bed, and in return is shown the trade.

crew_count_scribes.observation: A scribe stands by the work with a tablet, counting each crew by name as it comes and goes.

gangs_of_ten.observation: Workers are counted off in tens, and each ten answers to a foreman who answers for its work and its rations.

rotating_named_gangs.observation: Gangs with names like 'Friends of the King' work their watch on the great work, go home, and are relieved by the next gang.
rotating_named_gangs.social_consequence: Named gangs compete to finish their stretch of the work; pride in the gang keeps rotating levies coming back.

flood_season_great_works.observation: When the river covers the fields and farming stops, the idle hands are called up to haul stone for the great works.

workers_villages.observation: Beside the great work stands a walled village of bakeries, breweries and barracks where the builders eat, sleep and are tended.
workers_villages.social_consequence: A whole village of bakers, brewers, carriers and builders lives beside the great work, fed and housed by it.

measured_plot_allotment.observation: Fields are measured in rods and each worker is given a plot of known size to plough, sow or reap.

brick_quotas.observation: Each moulder owes so many hundred bricks a day, and the overseer counts the drying rows at sunset.

hired_harvest_hands.observation: At harvest the estates hire extra hands for the month, paid in grain, so the crop is cut before it sheds.

daily_task_norms.observation: A day's work is now fixed: so many cubits of earth dug, so many loads carried, and every overseer uses the same figures.
daily_task_norms.social_consequence: A day's work now has a number; whole projects are planned in man-days, and a worker who falls short is noticed.

light_duty_for_infirm.observation: The sick and the old are set to lighter work and keep their ration, so no one starves for having fallen ill.

man_day_accounts.observation: Scribes add up the days owed and the days worked for every crew, and the balance carries into the next year.
man_day_accounts.social_consequence: Labor becomes a written account like grain or silver, and those who keep the accounts can demand what is owed.

hired_labor_contracts.observation: A sealed tablet names the worker, the days, the task and the wage in barley or silver, before witnesses.
hired_labor_contracts.social_consequence: Labor can now be bought: the wealthy hire for grain or silver, and a class of people who own only their hands appears.

monthly_rest_days.observation: Every tenth day, and on the feasts of the month, the crews are stood down and go home.

levy_substitutes.observation: A man who owes the levy but can spare the grain pays another to go and dig in his place.

levy_exemptions.observation: Temple craftsmen and the king's smiths are written off the levy lists, for their work is owed elsewhere.

attendance_lists.observation: Each morning the foreman reads the names of his crew and marks who is present, who is sick and who has run.

trade_elders.observation: The eldest master of each trade speaks for the workshop crews before the palace stewards.

apprentice_quotas.observation: A master may take only so many apprentices, and each must be taught to the standard of the trade.

crew_loans_between_cities.observation: A city famed for its masons sends a crew to raise an allied ruler's temple, and they bring their methods home.
